## Goal

Distinguish changed sensitivity, additive interference and native-analyte loss;
calculate incremental spike recovery; and use a fixed-final-volume standard
addition without confusing its negative intercept with an ordinary high-sample
extrapolation. State which evidence a late spike can and cannot provide.

## Background

All signals in the supplied standard-addition data are already background
corrected. Each flask contains the same 10.00 mL sample made to 25.00 mL total.
Added-analyte concentration refers to this final volume. Under an additive
linear model with shared native/spike sensitivity,

$$y=b\left(c_s\frac{V_s}{V_f}+c_{added,final}\right)=a+b c_{added,final}.$$

The negative x-intercept is $x_0=-a/b$; its magnitude estimates native analyte
**in the diluted final flask**, so $c_s=-x_0V_f/V_s$. A constant unrelated signal
also shifts the intercept unless independently corrected. A successful spike
after extraction never passed through earlier native losses. The simulated
course data are separate analytical scenarios, not a validation of a real assay.

## By hand

**B1.** Equal-final-volume unspiked/spiked solutions give external-calibration
estimates 1.50 and 2.25 mg/L after adding 1.00 mg/L in the final flask. Calculate
incremental recovery and state what those units refer to. [Hint](#hint-b1)

**B2.** Equal 10.00 mL sample aliquots made to 25.00 mL give the fitted line
$y=0.3004+0.1496c_{added,final}$. Calculate x-intercept and original concentration.
Why is zero added analyte not a zero-analyte blank? [Hint](#hint-b2)

**B3.** A second design uses 5.00 mL sample made to 20.00 mL and gives
$y=0.240+0.120c_{added,final}$. Calculate the original concentration. Would the
same formula work without adjustment if final volumes differed between flasks?
[Hint](#hint-b3)

**B4.** Native analyte loses half its amount before a freely dissolved spike
is added. Native recovered and added material then give equal response. Can
late-spike recovery be 100%? Would that establish native recovery?
[Hint](#hint-b4)

## In R

Run this workflow at the project root in a fresh R session. Use standard-addition
and external standards in their correct separate tables.

```r
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
additions <- read_csv("data/course/standard-addition.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
external <- read_csv("data/course/external-matrix.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
fit_sa <- lm(blank_corrected_signal ~ spike_mg_l_final, data = additions)
fit_ext <- lm(blank_corrected_signal ~ c_mg_l, data = external)
a_sa <- unname(coef(fit_sa)[1]); b_sa <- unname(coef(fit_sa)[2])
x_intercept <- -a_sa / b_sa
original_sa_mg_l <- -x_intercept * 25.00 / 10.00
original_external_mg_l <- unname(
  (additions$blank_corrected_signal[1] - coef(fit_ext)[1]) / coef(fit_ext)[2]) * 25 / 10
line <- data.frame(spike_mg_l_final = seq(-2.3, 2.2, length.out = 100)) |>
  mutate(blank_corrected_signal = a_sa + b_sa * spike_mg_l_final)
ggplot(additions, aes(spike_mg_l_final, blank_corrected_signal)) +
  geom_point() + geom_line(data = line) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Added analyte in final flask (mg/L)", y = "Background-corrected signal") +
  theme_minimal()
spikes <- read_csv("data/course/spike-recovery.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
spike_recovery_percent <- 100 * diff(spikes$externally_estimated_mg_l_final) /
                               diff(spikes$added_mg_l_final)
answers <- data.frame(standard_addition_mg_l = original_sa_mg_l,
                      external_mg_l = original_external_mg_l,
                      incremental_recovery_percent = spike_recovery_percent)
answers
write_csv(answers, "output/matrix-recovery-exercise.csv")
```

**R1.** Read the x-intercept and volume correction with units. Explain why
negative analyte is not physically prepared. [Hint](#hint-r1)

**R2.** Compare the two fitted slopes and original concentration estimates.
Explain why an external standard can be precisely prepared yet inappropriate
for this sample. [Hint](#hint-r2)

**R3.** Does the fitted intercept's ordinary response interval automatically
give an interval for original concentration? Identify the uncertain inputs and
one assumption that could invalidate a straight-line standard-addition answer.
[Hint](#hint-r3)

## Hints

::: {#hint-b1 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="B1: use the increment, not the full spiked result"}
Subtract the unspiked estimate from the spiked estimate, then divide by the
known added concentration on the same final-volume basis.
:::
::: {#hint-b2 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="B2: first find the diluted native concentration"}
Solve $0=a+b x_0$ and multiply its magnitude by $25/10$. The unspiked sample
already contains native analyte.
:::
::: {#hint-b3 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="B3: the sample fraction is part of the model"}
Use $V_f/V_s=4$. Different final volumes change both native concentration and
matrix fraction across the series.
:::
::: {#hint-b4 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="B4: trace the spike path"}
The added analyte was not present during the loss. It can test later response
without testing earlier recovery.
:::
::: {#hint-e1 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="E1: the shared slope cancels"}
The intercept and slope both scale under the same multiplicative effect;
their ratio does not. An unrelated additive term behaves differently.
:::
::: {#hint-e2 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="E2: recovered is not original"}
At five mg/L original and half native recovery, the later prepared material
represents only 2.5 mg/L on the original-sample basis.
:::
::: {#hint-e3 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="E3: a line does not identify its intercept components"}
The intercept contains native response plus the additive term. Removing the
latter requires evidence beyond merely fitting additions.
:::
::: {#hint-r1 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="R1: model-based extrapolation"}
The negative x-axis position is inferred from the additive response model.
It is not an ordinary unknown measured beyond its external calibration.
:::
::: {#hint-r2 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="R2: compare sensitivities"}
Read [`coef`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/coef.html) for each model. A slope difference
changes the response per concentration even with an apparently excellent fit.
:::
::: {#hint-r3 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="R3: propagate through the ratio"}
Original concentration uses intercept divided by slope and a volume ratio.
Their covariance and volume uncertainties matter; a forward response interval
has a different target.
:::

## Solutions

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Full worked solutions"}
**B1.** Increment is $2.25-1.50=0.75$ mg/L. Divide by the added 1.00 mg/L and
multiply by 100 to obtain **75%**. Both concentrations refer to final solutions
with equal total volume and sample fraction, so the difference isolates an
increment under the stated matched design.

**B2.** $x_0=-0.3004/0.1496=-2.0080214$ mg/L final. Original concentration is
$2.0080214\times25/10=\mathbf{5.0200535}$ mg/L. An aliquot with no added
standard still contains the sample's native analyte, so it is not a zero-analyte
blank.

**B3.** $x_0=-2.00$ mg/L final; multiply by four to get **8.00 mg/L original**.
Different final volumes require an appropriate volume-corrected model. The
fixed-volume intercept formula cannot be reused as though the matrix fraction
and native concentration were constant.

**B4.** Yes: added material can respond quantitatively after the loss, giving
100% incremental recovery. It did not experience the loss and cannot establish
native recovery. A successful post-extraction spike is not a mass balance for
the original material.

**E1.** At default five mg/L original, standard addition returns **5.000 mg/L**
while external calibration returns **3.750 mg/L** in the exact demo model.
The sensitivity is suppressed from 0.200 to 0.150. Shared scaling cancels in
intercept/slope, but external calibration uses the wrong slope.

**E2.** At ratio one and 50% native recovery, standard addition returns
**2.500 mg/L**, yet late-spike recovery is **100%**. All later response is
correct; the input already lost analyte. No calibration can reconstruct that
loss without additional recovery evidence.

**E3.** With ratio 0.75, complete recovery and additive signal 0.120, the
intercept increases and the standard-addition estimate becomes **7.000 mg/L**
although the native truth is 5.000. Perfect independent subtraction returns it
to 5.000. This assumes the interferent was separately established under relevant
conditions; a reagent blank need not reveal a sample-specific signal. Exact
linearity did not distinguish the two intercept contributions.

**R1.** The supplied noisy teaching data give **5.02005 mg/L original** via the
negative final-flask intercept −2.00802 mg/L. Negative concentration is not
prepared; its location follows from the specified additive response model with
fixed sample fraction, not a licence to extrapolate every calibration.

**R2.** External slope is **0.1998**, matrix slope **0.1496** signal units per
mg/L. The external estimate is **3.76126 mg/L original**, lower than the
standard-addition estimate. Standard preparation precision cannot establish
sample matrix compatibility. The separate spike data give **75%** incremental
recovery.

**R3.** No. The inferred quantity depends on $a/b$ and $V_f/V_s$, so uncertainty
in both coefficients (including covariance) and volumes must be propagated.
A forward response interval for $a$ is not an inverse original-concentration
interval. Nonlinear response, changing sample fraction, residual additive
interference or different native/spike behaviour can invalidate the model.
This exercise therefore reports a conditional point estimate, not a complete
uncertainty interval.
:::
